content.title: About
content.content: Whole chocolate milk is a beverage made from whole cow's milk to which cocoa powder, sugar, and sometimes vanilla are added. It has a rich chocolate flavor, creamy texture, and contains all the nutrients found in whole milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate milk first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as a popular children's drink.
The fat content of whole chocolate milk is typically 3.5%–4%.
The cocoa powder used is rich in flavonoids, which may provide antioxidant benefits.
In some countries chocolate milk is classified as a "food supplement" and sold in large cartons for school cafeterias.
A darker chocolate taste is achieved with higher cocoa content and less sugar.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Whole milk is high in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chocolate milk provides riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Protein
items.content: A serving delivers about 8 g of high‑quality protein for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Cocoa flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids may improve vascular function and offer modest antioxidant effects.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Sugar and fat give an immediate energy boost, making the drink popular with children and athletes.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Added sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People who are lactose intolerant may experience digestive discomfort.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein or whey can occur in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Whole chocolate milk provides roughly 150 kcal per 250 ml, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink it cold as a refreshing beverage, blend it into smoothies, add it to oatmeal, or use it as a base for dessert sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Crackers are dry, crunchy baked products made from flour, water and a small amount of fat. They are often enjoyed as a light snack or as an accompaniment to soups, salads and cheeses. The water in the dough provides the necessary moisture and helps create the characteristic porous texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crackers appeared in Europe in the 19th century as a lighter alternative to bread.
There are many varieties: wheat, rye, corn and gluten‑free flours are used.
Crackers are a staple in military rations because of their long shelf life.
In some countries they are served with cheese, cold cuts or pâté as a "tapas" style snack.
Thin crackers can be flavored with herbs, spices or cheese.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Most crackers contain little fat and calories, making them a convenient snack for weight management.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: The flour provides slowly released energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions are rich in dietary fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Pairs well with protein
items.content: Crackers are often served with cheese, ham or nut spreads, enhancing their nutritional profile.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Water in the recipe helps maintain optimal product moisture and aids nutrient absorption.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some crackers are high in salt, which may be unsuitable for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat‑based crackers are not suitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Recipes may contain dairy, soy or nuts, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: If stored too long, crackers can become soft or stale, so checking the expiration date is important.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be eaten plain, spread with cream cheese, hummus, pâté, or used as a base for canapés. They are commonly served alongside soups, salads and cheeses. For best flavor, keep them in a dry place.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent moisture buildup and spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit Nectar NFS is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from concentrated fruit juice diluted with water and lightly sweetened. It offers a rich, aromatic flavor without artificial colors or flavors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: NFS stands for “Natural Fruit Syrup,” a term used in beverage production.
The nectar retains most of the vitamins and minerals of the original fruits thanks to gentle heat processing.
Unlike pure juice, nectar has a longer shelf life without the need for preservatives.
The NFS range includes orange, apple, berry blend, and tropical fruit variants.
PET bottle packaging provides easy transport and recyclability.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Fruit nectar is rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: High water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance, especially in hot weather.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: A small amount of soluble fiber aids normal digestion.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Simple sugars quickly replenish energy stores, making it convenient after physical activity.

items.title: Rich fruit aroma
items.content: Natural aromatic compounds enhance taste and can improve mood.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Nectar contains added sugar, so people with diabetes or weight concerns should limit intake.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to specific fruits may react to nectar made from those fruits.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Highly acidic variants (e.g., citrus) may irritate the stomach lining if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Nectar is ready to drink straight from the bottle. It can be enjoyed chilled, used in cocktails, mixed with water 1:1, or added to desserts and sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the nectar in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: A vanilla ice cream sandwich consists of two soft waffle cookies with creamy vanilla ice cream sandwiched between them. It is a popular snack often sold in packs of 2–4 pieces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first ice cream sandwich appeared in the United States in the 1960s as a convenient summer treat.
Vanilla is considered the most neutral flavor and is often used as a base for adding various fillings and toppings.
The waffle cookies are usually made without added sugar to let the ice cream’s sweetness shine.
Ice cream sandwiches are commonly packaged in individual boxes, making them ideal for vending machines and street kiosks.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Vanilla ice cream contains dairy, which provides calcium important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: The sandwich delivers fast energy through carbohydrates from the cookies and sugar in the ice cream, useful during active days.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dairy ingredients and a small amount of egg in the cookie batter supply vitamins B2 and B12.

items.title: Milk and gluten allergy
items.content: The sandwich contains milk and wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with those allergies.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sugar in the ice cream and cookies makes the product calorie‑dense; people with diabetes should limit consumption.

items.title: Melting at high temperatures
items.content: Storing above ‑ 18 °C causes the ice cream to melt quickly, which can lead to bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be eaten straight from the package after a quick chill in the freezer. Optionally, slice it and add fresh berries, nuts, or chocolate sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at ‑ 18 °C or lower. Once removed from the package, it should be consumed within 30 minutes to prevent melting.

content.title: About
content.content: Similac NFS (Newborn Feeding System) is an infant formula designed for newborns and babies up to 6 months. The formula provides an optimal balance of proteins, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals in line with WHO recommendations and FDA standards.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Similac is one of the most widely used infant nutrition brands in the US and Europe.
The NFS formula is enriched with DHA and ARA – fatty acids important for brain and eye development.
It contains the prebiotic FOS (fructooligosaccharides) to support a healthy gut microbiome.
Each batch undergoes double quality testing: during manufacturing and before market release.

items.title: Supports growth and development
items.content: A balanced protein and energy profile promotes normal weight gain and linear growth in infants.

items.title: Brain development
items.content: DHA and ARA help form neural connections and support visual function.

items.title: Gut health
items.content: The FOS prebiotic encourages growth of beneficial bacteria, improving digestion.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamins A, C, E and zinc strengthen the infant’s immune system.

items.title: Easy digestibility
items.content: A special protein processing technology reduces the risk of allergic reactions.

items.title: Cow‑milk protein allergy
items.content: Infants with a confirmed allergy to cow‑milk protein may react to this formula.

items.title: Incorrect reconstitution
items.content: Over‑concentrated formula can cause dehydration, while overly diluted formula may lead to nutrient deficiency.

items.title: Storage after preparation
items.content: Prepared formula left at room temperature for more than 2 hours should be discarded to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Mix the specified amount of powder with freshly boiled water cooled to 37 °C. Stir thoroughly until the mixture is smooth and free of lumps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, use within 4 weeks. Prepared formula can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat with gravy is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of boiled or roasted meat covered with a flavorful thick sauce. Common meats are beef, pork or chicken, and the gravy is made from broth, cream, tomato base or a blend of spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Serving meat with gravy dates back to medieval European kitchens, where gravy was used to moisten dry cuts of meat.
In different regions the gravy can be light (cream‑based) or dark (made from browned meat and tomato paste).
In Japan a similar concept is “nitsuke,” a sauce served with grilled meat.
Gravy helps retain moisture in the meat, keeping it juicy during longer storage.
Some countries add red wine to the gravy, giving it a distinctive aroma.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and pork are high in vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Meat supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Gravy, especially when cream‑based, adds calories, useful for people with higher energy needs.

items.title: Improved nutrient absorption
items.content: Fats in the gravy aid the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Rich creamy gravies can contribute to weight gain if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared gravies often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some gravies include dairy, gluten or soy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Risk of bacterial growth
items.content: Improper storage of cooked meat can lead to pathogen growth, so keep the product refrigerated.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a main course, typically with a side of potatoes, rice or vegetables. Reheat in the microwave or on the stovetop, stirring to keep the gravy from separating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage freeze at –18 °C, where it remains good for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before consumption.

potato-boiled-from-fresh-peel-eaten-made.title: Boiled Potato, fresh, peel eaten, with margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Boiled potato is a dish made from fresh potatoes cooked in salted water until tender, with the skin left on and eaten. Margarine is often added for a mild, buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato is the fourth most produced food crop worldwide after cereals, rice, and wheat.
Eating the skin retains most of the fiber and nutrients, especially vitamin C and potassium.
Margarine is used instead of butter because it contains less saturated fat and is more stable at high temperatures.
Boiled potatoes serve as a base for many dishes: salads, mash, casseroles, and side dishes.
Large potatoes take longer to cook, so they are often cut into uniform pieces for even boiling.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide slowly digestible carbs that help maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium supports fluid balance, heart function, and muscle activity.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in the skin boosts immunity and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The peel is high in fiber, which aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Boiled potatoes themselves contain almost no fat; adding margarine lets you control the amount.

items.title: Margarine allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to vegetable oils or additives used in margarine.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is commonly added during boiling; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high GI, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Prolonged heating in water can produce small amounts of acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve boiled potatoes warm, drizzled with melted margarine and seasoned with fresh herbs, salt, or spices. The skin can be eaten together with the flesh, adding texture and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool boiled potatoes to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the microwave or on the stove, adding fresh margarine before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Sunflower seeds are the edible seeds of the sunflower plant (Helianthus annuus), which is native to North America. Each seed is enclosed in a striped shell, and the kernel inside has a mild, nutty flavor. They are eaten roasted or raw as a snack and used in baking, salads, and spreads, and they are also a source of sunflower oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sunflowers were cultivated by Indigenous peoples of North America long before they spread to Europe.
Botanically, what we call a sunflower seed is a fruit called an achene, with the shell as its outer layer.
A single sunflower head can contain hundreds to thousands of seeds.
Sunflower seeds are popular as a snack in many countries, especially in Eastern Europe and Central Asia.
Young sunflower heads track the sun during growth, a behavior called heliotropism.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Sunflower seeds are one of the best food sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: They contain mostly unsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Sunflower seeds provide magnesium, selenium, zinc, and copper.

items.title: Source of protein and fiber
items.content: Shelled seeds provide plant protein and fiber, which support fullness.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: They provide thiamin, folate, and vitamin B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Sunflower seeds are calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Sodium in flavored varieties
items.content: Salted or flavored seeds may contain a lot of sodium.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Sunflower seed allergy is uncommon but can occur.

items.title: Cadmium and shells
items.content: Sunflower seeds can absorb cadmium from soil, so very large regular amounts are not recommended. Cracking shells with the teeth may damage them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Shelled sunflower seeds can be sprinkled on salads, yogurt, oatmeal, and soups, or added to bread, granola, and baked goods. They can be ground into sunflower seed butter or used in pesto. Seeds in the shell are a popular snack, with the shell discarded.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sunflower seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dark place. Because of their oil content, shelled seeds can turn rancid, so refrigerate or freeze them for longer storage. Discard seeds that smell sharp, bitter, or like paint.
